_about: Notes for the ingredients knowledge file. Edit freely; run tools/build_knowledge.py afterwards.

lentils-red.note: Split, skinless lentils that cook fast and melt into soup (shorbat adas). No soaking. Simmer 15 to 20 minutes in about three times their volume of water.

lentils-brown.note: Whole lentils that hold their shape, for kabsa, mujaddara and salads. No soaking. Simmer 25 to 30 minutes.

green-peas-dry.note: Whole dried peas: soak overnight, then simmer 45 to 60 minutes. Split peas need no soaking and take 30 to 40 minutes. Check which one the pack holds.

mung-beans.note: No soaking needed, though 2 to 4 hours speeds them up. Simmer 30 to 40 minutes. Good in soups and with rice.

black-eyed-beans.note: Cook without soaking in 40 to 50 minutes, or about 30 minutes after a few hours of soaking.

kidney-beans-dry.note: Soak 8 to 12 hours, then boil hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering 60 to 90 minutes. Raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin, so never slow-cook them from raw.

white-beans-dry.note: Soak 8 to 12 hours and simmer 60 to 90 minutes until creamy. Classic in tomato stews.

chickpeas-dry.note: Soak 8 to 12 hours (a pinch of baking soda helps), then simmer 60 to 90 minutes, or about 30 minutes in a pressure cooker. Much cheaper than canned; cook a big batch and freeze it.

chana-dal.note: Split, skinned chickpeas. Soak 30 minutes to 2 hours, then simmer 30 to 45 minutes. Good in soups and dals.

chickpeas-canned.note: Ready to use. Drain and rinse to cut the salt. A 380 to 400 g can gives roughly 240 g of chickpeas.

foul-canned.note: Cooked fava beans. Warm with garlic, lemon, cumin and tahini for breakfast. Rinse if you want less salt.

kidney-beans-canned.note: Already cooked and safe to use straight away. Drain and rinse.

white-beans-canned.note: Drain and rinse. Good in salads and quick stews.

hummus-canned.note: Ready-made hummus with tahini. Usually vegan; check the label for dairy.

oats.note: Rolled oats cook in about 5 minutes, or soak overnight. Only gluten-free if the pack says so.

rice-basmati.note: Rinse until the water runs clear. About 1 cup rice to 1½ cups water, 15 to 20 minutes, then rest 5 minutes.

pasta.note: Dry durum-wheat pasta is usually egg-free. Check the label, especially for fresh or egg pasta.

bulgur.note: Fine bulgur: soak in boiling water for 10 to 15 minutes (for tabbouleh). Coarse bulgur: simmer in twice its volume of water for 12 to 15 minutes.

freekeh.note: Roasted green wheat with a smoky taste. Cracked freekeh takes about 2½ times its volume of water and 20 to 25 minutes; whole freekeh about 45 minutes.

quinoa.note: Rinse first to remove the bitter coating. One part quinoa to two parts water, 15 minutes, then rest 5.

tahini.note: Ground sesame paste. Stir the oil back in before using and keep it somewhere cool. Adds calcium and protein to sauces, oats and dips.

peanut-butter.note: The best ones are just peanuts and salt. Some brands add honey or whey, so check the label.

peanuts.note: One of the cheapest protein snacks. Choose unsalted for everyday eating.

almonds.note: Good for calcium and vitamin E. Toast in a dry pan for salads.

pumpkin-seeds.note: Among the highest-protein seeds. Toast lightly and sprinkle on salads or oats.

chia.note: Soak 1 tablespoon in 3 tablespoons of water for 15 minutes to make a gel, or stir into oats. A plant source of omega-3.

sesame.note: Toast lightly before using. Sprinkle on oats, salads and bread.

oat-milk.note: Low in protein. If it replaces dairy milk, pick one fortified with calcium and vitamin B12.

almond-milk.note: Low in protein and calories. Pick one fortified with calcium and vitamin B12.

bread-arabic.note: Cheap and filling. Most plain Arabic bread is vegan, but some recipes use milk, so check the label.

tortilla-brown.note: Check the label for milk or whey.

dates.note: A natural sweetener for oats, smoothies and snacks. Khalas and Sukkari are common, affordable varieties.

tomato.note: Its vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from beans and lentils.

onion.note: The base of most savory dishes here. A bag is the cheapest way to buy.

lemon.note: Its vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from beans and lentils, which is one reason Saudi cooking pairs them so well.

garlic.note: Buy loose by weight for the best price.

cucumber.note: For salads, and with hummus or foul at breakfast.

bell-pepper.note: Adds vitamin C to bean dishes, which helps iron absorption.

zucchini.note: Roast or stuff it; cooks quickly.

parsley.note: Bought by the bunch; very cheap.

mint.note: Bought by the bunch; for salads and tea.

coriander.note: Fresh coriander (cilantro), bought by the bunch.

carrot.note: Adds sweetness and color to soups and stews.

celery.note: Adds savory depth to soups and stews.

green-onion.note: Bought by the bunch; for salads.

spinach.note: Rich in folate and iron. Eat with lemon or tomato to absorb more of the iron. Frozen spinach works in cooked dishes.

avocado.note: Healthy fats. Good on beans and rice.

tomato-paste.note: Concentrated tomato for kabsa-style dishes and stews.

tomatoes-canned.note: Use in soups and stews when tomato sauce isn't available.

olive-oil.note: For dressings and finishing. Vegetable oil is cheaper for frying.

cumin.note: Goes with almost every bean and lentil dish here.

black-pepper.note: Buy loose or in small packs; it loses aroma over time.

cardamom.note: For Arabic coffee, rice and oats. Buying whole and grinding keeps it fresh.

chili-powder.note: Spice mixes vary: some kabsa and bharat mixes contain chicken stock powder, so check the label.

date-syrup.note: A local sweetener for dressings, oats and tahini (dibs w tahini).

vinegar.note: For dressings and pickles; lemon juice works instead in most recipes.
